title: Máine Mór comes west
claim: The kingdom's own story tells of Máine Mór leading his people west to settle beyond the Shannon, and of a victory at Claenloch that secured the land. This is told as tradition, not record.
reference: Origin tradition (Curley; O'Donovan 1843). Claenloch 538 per later tradition

title: The ruling lines settle
claim: Several branches of the dynasty share and contest the kingship, and the kingdom takes shape across the Suck valley.

title: Murchad, king of Uí Maine
claim: The annals record the death of Murchad son of Áed, king of Uí Maine. In this era the ruling line came to be known as Uí Chellaig, after an earlier king named Cellach.
reference: Annals of Inisfallen AI962.3; AFM M960 (year)

title: Tadg Mór at Clontarf
claim: Tadg Mór Ua Cellaig fights beside Brian Bórama at Clontarf and is remembered among the fallen, a proud memory for the family.

title: The Suck is dug
claim: The Annals of Tigernach record that Toirrdelbach Ó Conchobair, king of Connacht, had the river Suck dug out by a great muster of Connacht men, so that it flooded two marshes into lakes on its way to Lough Ree. In the same year he built bridges at Athlone and at Dún Leodha (Ballinasloe) on the Suck.
reference: Annals of Tigernach T1139.4 (the Suck dug by Toirrdelbach); AFM M1139 (bridges at Athlone and Dún Leodha on the Suck)

title: A church at Clonmacnoise
claim: Conchobar Ua Ceallaigh and the people of Uí Maine build a church at Clonmacnoise, still remembered as O'Kelly's Church: a sign of the kingdom's close ties to the great monastery across the Shannon.
reference: Annals of the Four Masters M1167 (church at Clonmacnoise by Conchobar Ua Ceallaigh)

title: Tadg at Athenry
ga: Tadhg ag Baile Átha an Rí
claim: On 10 August 1316 Tadg Ó Ceallaigh, king of Uí Maine, falls at Athenry with many of his kin. The annals remember him as the man the Gaels hoped most from in his time. The lordship regroups around its core.
reference: Annals of the Four Masters M1316; Annals of Connacht 1316

title: The great Christmas feast
claim: Uilliam Buide Ó Ceallaigh welcomes the poets, judges, historians and musicians of Ireland for Christmas at his court at Pallas, and Gofraidh Fionn Ó Dálaigh praises it in verse.
reference: Poem: Knott, Ériu 5 (1911) 50–69; Bardic Poetry Database poem 932. Lios Mór at Pallas = the Ó Ceallaigh pailís: FitzPatrick, Landscapes of the Learned pp. 147–149. Feast held at Pallas: this site's reading, awaiting FitzPatrick p. 148
pinned: Ériu 5 pp. 50–69 (poem); FitzPatrick pp. 147–149 (Pallas = pailís); feast site awaiting p. 148

title: Kilconnell Friary
claim: Uilliam founds a Franciscan friary at Kilconnell, a stone centre of learning and prayer at the heart of the lordship.
reference: Annals of the Four Masters M1353.7

title: Widest extent
claim: Around 1380 to 1420 the lordship is at its broadest, from Athlone and Roscommon to Abbeyknockmoy and Tiaquin, with Ballinasloe and Tycooly (Ticooly) inside it. The solid core is well attested; the hatched outer band is the claimed reach.
reference: Curley, PhD thesis (widest extent c. 1380–1420; c. 1,706 km²)

title: Knockdoe
claim: A great battle near Knockdoe draws in lords from across Connacht and beyond, with Ó Ceallaigh at its heart.
reference: Annals of the Four Masters M1504.13–14

title: The lordship ends
claim: The lordship of Uí Mhaine ended with the Tudor changes of the late 1500s and the land settlements of the early 1600s. Its names, townlands, poems and stones remain, and that is what this site celebrates.
